opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the honest answer is that we look at it from a few different angles, because a single benchmark number can hide a lot.

The first thing we do is compare against the supervised fine-tuned checkpoint we started from, on the same held-out set of tool-calling tasks. That gives us the headline: did success rate go up? But then we break it down. Is the model picking the right tool more often? Is it filling in arguments correctly, with the right types and formats? Is it chaining multiple calls in the right order? And, really important, is it knowing when *not* to call a tool, when it should just answer directly or ask a clarifying question?

What we often found is that RL didn't so much teach the model new knowledge as sharpen behaviors it already sort of had. With SFT, the model has seen examples of good tool use, but it's imitating. With RL, especially with verifiable rewards where you can actually execute the call and check the result, it learns from its own mistakes. So you see big gains in things like argument correctness and recovering after a tool returns an error, because those are exactly the cases where the reward signal is crisp.

We also read a lot of trajectories by hand. That sounds unglamorous, but it's where you catch reward hacking. Sometimes the score goes up because the model found a shortcut, like producing outputs that pass the checker without really solving the task, or calling tools redundantly because that happened to correlate with reward. So we'll sample rollouts before and after and look at what changed qualitatively.

And then we check for regressions: general capabilities, instruction following, the length and verbosity of responses. RL can make a model narrower if you're not careful, so we want to be sure we gained tool-calling ability without giving up something else. If the gains hold up on tasks and tool schemas the model never saw during training, that's when we're actually confident the improvement is real and not just overfitting to the environment.

r001.rationale: It mentions chaining multiple calls in the right order and recovering from tool errors, but does not state that a later tool call is chosen based on a previous tool’s response.

r002.rationale: It says RL sharpened behaviors the model already had and contrasts RL with imitation from SFT examples, but does not say multi-turn tool-calling behavior emerged without researchers curating examples of it.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the honest answer is that it's harder than it sounds, because the thing you're optimizing against during training and the thing you actually care about are not the same object. We started with a model that was already pretty decent at tool calling from supervised fine-tuning, and the question was really, what did RL buy us on top of that?

The first thing we look at is the obvious stuff, the benchmarks, things like the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard, tau-bench, our own internal evals. And you do see the numbers go up. But I'm always a little suspicious of that in isolation, because RL is very good at finding whatever your reward is measuring, and if your eval is correlated with your reward, you've kind of just measured your own training signal twice.

So what we found more useful was to slice the failures. Before RL, the dominant failure modes were things like calling a tool when it shouldn't have, or hallucinating a parameter that wasn't in the schema, or picking the right tool but getting the argument format wrong. After RL, a lot of those structural errors basically disappear. The model learns very reliably to respect the schema, to not invent tools, to stop and ask when a required argument is missing. That's the easy part for RL, honestly, because it's verifiable, you can write a checker for it.

The harder part is multi-step behavior. Did the model learn to recover when a tool returns an error? Does it chain calls sensibly, or does it just fire off everything at once? Those are the places where we had to do a lot of manual inspection, actually reading trajectories, because the aggregate metrics would say things improved but you want to see whether it improved for the right reasons or whether it just learned some shortcut in the environment.

And then the last thing, which I think people underweight, is checking what got worse. RL on tool calling can make a model overly eager to use tools, so you have to hold out conversational data and plain reasoning tasks and make sure you didn't regress there. If I had to summarize, I'd say the assessment is less about one number and more about building a taxonomy of behaviors and watching how each one moves.

r001.rationale: The response raises recovery after a tool error and sensible call chaining as behaviors to inspect, but does not state that reinforcement learning enabled a subsequent call based on a tool’s response.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that reinforcement learning produced multi-turn tool-calling behavior without researchers explicitly curating examples of it.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate two questions: did the model get better at calling tools, and did that help it solve the user’s task? For the first, you can look at whether it chose the right tool, supplied the right arguments, and used the result appropriately. For the second, you need to evaluate the full interaction—did it actually accomplish what the user asked?

To isolate the contribution of reinforcement learning, I’d compare the checkpoint before RL with the checkpoint after RL on the same held-out tasks, with the same tools and inference budget. And I’d look at the trajectories, not just the aggregate score. Is it recovering from a tool error? Is it avoiding unnecessary calls? Is it recognizing when it has enough information to answer? Those comparisons help distinguish an improvement in task-solving behavior from simply getting better at the particular reward you trained against.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that RL produced multi-turn tool-calling behavior without researchers explicitly curating examples of it.

sol-6.1.text:
We try to separate two things: did the model choose the right tool and call it correctly, and did that actually help it complete the task? A tool call can be perfectly valid and still be the wrong thing to do.

So we compare the model before and after reinforcement learning on held-out tasks, looking at end-to-end success as well as the individual decisions along the way. Does it supply the right arguments? Does it use the result correctly? If a call fails, can it recover? And does it know when it already has enough information to answer?

The important question is whether it’s becoming more effective at solving the user’s problem, rather than simply becoming more likely to call a tool.
